AmiBSDNet 0.4
=============

AmiBSDNet is a TCP/IP network stack for AmigaOS 3.1 and later
(Workbench 3.2 recommended), built from the networking code of the
NetBSD 11 kernel: the real BSD TCP/IP, IPv4 and IPv6 implementation,
running as a "rump kernel" on top of Exec. Programs use it through the
standard bsdsocket.library (AmiTCP / Roadshow API), so existing Amiga
network software works without changes.

Requirements
------------
- a 68020 or better CPU; a PiStorm (Emu68) is the main target
- Fast RAM: the stack uses about 3.5 MB, all of it Fast RAM (no Chip RAM)
- a network card with a SANA-II driver. The PiStorm's Wi-Fi driver
  (wifipi.device) is included; WinUAE: uaenet.device; Zorro cards such
  as the A2065, Ariadne or X-Surf: their own driver
- no other TCP/IP stack running at the same time (the installer offers
  to take an installed one out of the boot)

Installation
------------
Double-click "Install". First the installer looks for another TCP/IP
stack (Roadshow, Miami, AmiTCP, Genesis, or any bsdsocket.library on
disk). If one is found it offers to:

  Switch       its startup lines in S:Startup-Sequence and S:User-Startup
               are commented out ("; [AmiBSDNet] ..."), and its WBStartup
               items and LIBS:bsdsocket.library are moved to
               SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Disabled.
  Keep it      nothing is changed.

Switching is a trial. After the next boot AmiBSDNet has three minutes
to get connected. If it does, the switch stays. If it does not, it goes
back by itself ("NetCtrl FALLBACK"): the other stack and the Wi-Fi
driver and firmware it replaced are put back, AmiBSDNet is taken out of
the boot, its logs are saved in SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs, and a
requester asks you to reboot. You are never left without a network:
a trial boot that ends without a connection (the machine hangs, crashes
or is reset before AmiBSDNet has connected) also counts as failed, and
the next boot goes back by itself. So after switching, leave the
machine running until the status icon shows an address.
"NetCtrl FALLBACK" also goes back by hand at any time; once you are
happy with AmiBSDNet, "NetCtrl REMOVEOTHERS" deletes the other stack's
startup entries for good.

The startup files are saved as S:<name>.amibsdnet-backup before the
first change. Afterwards the installer checks again and tells you if
anything of the other stack would still be started at boot. AmiBSDNet
itself does not start while another stack is running (and never stops
the rest of S:User-Startup).

It then installs the programs, WirelessManager and, on a PiStorm, the
Wi-Fi driver wifipi.device with its firmware (DEVS:Networks,
DEVS:Firmware). What was there before is saved first, once:
wifipi.device.old and DEVS:Firmware.old.

The installer finds your network adapters by itself (every SANA-II driver in DEVS:Networks, and drivers built into
ROM such as WinUAE's uaenet.device) and tells Ethernet from Wi-Fi. If
you have both, both are set up. For Wi-Fi it asks for the network name
and passphrase (or leave them empty and choose the network later from
the status icon). It then asks whether your network uses DHCP (most do)
or a fixed address, and whether to show the status icon on the
Workbench. If no adapter is found you can choose the driver yourself.
It adds this line to S:User-Startup:

    C:AmiBSDNet

The stack starts in the background; boot is not delayed while it waits
for a DHCP server.

Ethernet and Wi-Fi together
---------------------------
Ethernet and Wi-Fi are separate interfaces that work at the same time,
each with its own address from its own network. Internet traffic goes
out through Ethernet while its cable is connected and through Wi-Fi
otherwise; the switch happens by itself when the cable is plugged in or
pulled. The name servers of both are used.

Cable and Wi-Fi changes
-----------------------
Nothing has to be started by hand. With DHCP, AmiBSDNet keeps asking
for an address in the background until it gets one, so a cable plugged
in or a router switched on after boot is picked up by itself. Drivers
that report link changes (SANA-II link events, e.g. Wi-Fi association)
make it react at once: the address is released when the link goes and
fetched again when it returns. The status icon shows "No cable" or
"No Wi-Fi" while there is no link.

Wi-Fi
-----
Wireless drivers such as Emu68's wifipi.device associate with the
network; the WPA handshake is done by WirelessManager (Neil Cafferkey's
wpa_supplicant port, installed to C:WirelessManager), which reads
ENV:Sys/Wireless.prefs. Both are included in this package (see
ThirdParty.txt for their authors and licences). AmiBSDNet starts WirelessManager itself for a
Wi-Fi interface if it is not already running. The installer asks for
the network name and passphrase; to change networks later, double-click
the status icon and choose Wi-Fi...: the window lists the networks in
range (strongest first), and Connect stores the network, restarts
WirelessManager and fetches a new address. A scan can be stopped with
Close; it gives up by itself after 30 seconds.

The status icon shows "Net: No Wi-Fi" until WirelessManager has joined
the network; DHCP starts as soon as it has. WirelessManager's messages
are in T:WirelessManager.log (more of them after "SetEnv AmiBSDNet/Debug
1" and a reboot). If the status window says "DRIVER NOT FOUND", the
driver named in the settings is not in DEVS:Networks.

The status icon
---------------
AmiBSDNetStatus puts an icon on the Workbench showing whether you are
online and your address (or "No cable", "No Wi-Fi", "Connecting").
Double-click it for a status window with Go Online / Go Offline,
Reconnect, Wi-Fi... (for Wi-Fi interfaces) and Settings.... The same
windows are in the Workbench Tools menu: "AmiBSDNet..." and "AmiBSDNet
Settings...".

The Settings window holds the whole configuration: the Ethernet and
Wi-Fi drivers (Detect finds them), automatic (DHCP) or fixed address,
gateway, DNS server, host name, and the Wi-Fi network and passphrase
(Scan... lists the networks in range). Save stores the settings and
applies them at once, without a reboot; Use applies them until the next
reboot. A fixed address is used for Ethernet if there is an Ethernet
adapter, else for Wi-Fi.

It is also the "AmiBSDNet" commodity
in Exchange: Show opens the status window, Enable / Disable switch the
network online / offline. Tool types: STACK=<command to start the
stack> (default C:AmiBSDNet), INTERVAL=<seconds between updates>.

Commands
--------
AmiBSDNet [CONFIG=<file>] [LOG=<file>] [DEBUG]
    Starts the stack. Configuration defaults to
    ENV:AmiBSDNet/AmiBSDNet.conf, the log to T:AmiBSDNet.log.

NetCtrl [STATUS|ONLINE|OFFLINE|RECONFIG|WAIT|PROBE|CHECK|...] [TIMEOUT=<s>]
    STATUS    interfaces, addresses, traffic counters, name servers
    ONLINE    bring the network up
    OFFLINE   take the network down
    RECONFIG  re-read the configuration file
    WAIT      wait until the network is up (for scripts)

NetCtrl PROBE
    Lists the network adapters and whether each is Ethernet or Wi-Fi;
    sets the variables AmiBSDNet/Ethernet and AmiBSDNet/WiFi.

NetCtrl CHECK
    Lists other installed TCP/IP stacks and what of them is still
    started at boot.

NetCtrl DISABLEOTHERS | REMOVEOTHERS | RESTOREOTHERS | FALLBACK
    Takes other TCP/IP stacks out of the boot (can be undone), removes
    their startup entries and files, or undoes DISABLEOTHERS. FALLBACK
    goes back completely: the other stack and the original Wi-Fi driver
    and firmware come back, AmiBSDNet is taken out of the boot, and its
    logs are saved in SYS:Storage/AmiBSDNet-Logs. Reboot afterwards.

Ping HOST [COUNT=<n>]
    Send ICMP echo requests.

Configuration file
------------------
ENVARC:AmiBSDNet/AmiBSDNet.conf (copied to ENV: at boot), one item per
line, '#' starts a comment:

    hostname   amiga
    interface  sana0 genet.device 0 dhcp
    interface  sana1 wifipi.device 0 dhcp wifi
    # or a fixed address:
    # interface  sana0 genet.device 0 address 192.168.1.20/24
    # gateway    192.168.1.1
    # nameserver 192.168.1.1
    domain     home.lan

Up to four interfaces (sana0 ... sana3) can be configured; the first
one that is connected carries the Internet traffic. "wifi" marks a
Wi-Fi interface for the Settings window (the stack also detects it from
the driver). With DHCP, the router and name servers come from the DHCP
server.

Host names are looked up in DEVS:Internet/hosts first, then with DNS.

Limitations of this version
---------------------------
- The stack cannot be unloaded once started (NetCtrl OFFLINE takes the
  network down); a reboot removes it.
- IPv6 is built in but not yet configured automatically.
- Not yet implemented bsdsocket.library calls fail with ENOSYS: the
  packet filter (bpf_*), mbuf and monitoring APIs, and Roadshow's
  interface and route configuration calls.
